summary: In Greek mythology, Nike (Ancient Greek: Νίκη, "Victory") is the personification and goddess of victory, in battle as well as in athletic, musical, and other contests. According to Hesiod's Theogony she is the daughter of the Titan Pallas and the Oceanid Styx, and the sister of Zelus, Kratos, and Bia. She is closely linked to Zeus and to Athena, and is usually depicted as a swift, winged figure. Her Roman counterpart is Victoria.
etymology: The name Nike (Νίκη) derives from the Greek noun níkē, meaning "victory" or the "upper hand" in battle or contest. The word's deeper origin is uncertain; it has been connected by some scholars to neîkos ("strife") and the verb neikeîn ("to quarrel").

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: In Hesiod's Theogony, Nike is the daughter of the Titan Pallas and the Oceanid Styx, the goddess of the underworld river. Her siblings are likewise personifications of abstract qualities: Zelus (Rivalry or Zeal), Kratos (Strength or Power), and Bia (Force).
Together this group of siblings came to be regarded as constant attendants of Zeus, embodying qualities that became permanently associated with his sovereignty.

sections.heading: Mythology and role
paragraphs: Nike and her siblings were among the first to side with Zeus in the Titanomachy, the war between the Olympians and the Titans. Hesiod relates that Styx brought her children to Zeus's aid, and that in return Zeus honoured them and kept them ever at his side, so that victory, strength, and force became lasting components of his authority.

Nike rarely possesses an independent narrative of her own; instead she functions as a companion and attribute of victory-granting deities, above all Zeus and Athena, and is frequently shown crowning victors or alighting beside them. In Nonnus's later epic Dionysiaca she appears at Zeus's side during his struggle against the monster Typhon, encouraging the god and shielding him in the fight.

sections.heading: Cult and worship
paragraphs: Nike's most prominent cult association is with Athena. At Athens, the goddess Athena Nike had a sanctuary on the Acropolis from the sixth century BC, and the small Temple of Athena Nike was built there in the later fifth century BC. The cult image was famously wingless (apteros); according to Pausanias the Athenians believed that, having no wings, Victory would always remain with them.

Nike is also connected to the worship of Zeus, particularly at Olympia, where she appears frequently on coinage minted from around 500 BC onward. As a divine figure granting success in war and in the games, she was a recurring presence in dedications and victory monuments.

sections.heading: Depictions in art
paragraphs: Nike is typically portrayed as winged and moving at great speed, often carrying a victory wreath, laurel branch, palm frond, or ribbon, and sometimes a libation bowl or trophy. She is a common motif on vases, coins, and architectural sculpture, where she crowns athletes, charioteers, and warriors.

Among the most celebrated sculptures of the goddess are the Nike of Paionios (c. 420 BC) at Olympia and the Hellenistic Winged Victory of Samothrace, which depicts Nike alighting upon the prow of a ship. In the Roman world she was identified with the goddess Victoria.
